newsitem.title: UK: PHYSICAL-FINANCIAL GOLD MARKETS ARE STILL TIED.
newsitem.headline: PHYSICAL-FINANCIAL GOLD MARKETS ARE STILL TIED.

text.p: Gold's physical and financial markets are inextricably bound together, according to stockbroker T. Hoare and Co partner Rhona O'Connell.
In remarks prepared for presentation at the International Gold Markets Conference in Istanbul, Turkey, on Tuesday, O'Connell demonstrated the linkage during the 1987 stock market boom and crash.
During that year the gold market moved into a supply surplus as mine production grew rapidly but physical offtake slowed due to lower official coin minting.

"The...surplus was absorbed very largely by fund managers who were hedged against overvalued stock markets and a bull run was sustained until November reflecting a combination of the physical and professional markets working in tandem," she said.
In 1993, while the physical market faded in response to higher prices (after booming physical offtake the previous year), investors and speculators took prices higher.

But after the "speculative froth " had gone, "it took only a matter of weeks before private physical buyers returned in sufficient force to maintain re-rating (of the price) at higher levels, O'Connell said.
Increasing speculation generally coincides with rising prices rather than falling prices. "Speculators will generally extend a trend, they will rarely determine one," she said.
However, the 1987 stock market crash brought a more precise dovetailing of the physical and financial gold markets than was immediately obvious.
When the stock markets crashed in October of that year, there was heavy activity in gold as some buyers attempted to avoid further equity market weakness.
However, there was also heavy selling of gold, she noted. This came from two sources, miners and speculators selling on to strength and also from the people who had used gold as a stock market hedge.

"It is important to note....that gold has a 48-hour settlement period which at the time was shorter than any equity market and so the necessary funds were available to equity investors in time to prevent meltdown," she said.
Now only the Hong Kong and South Korean stock markets have shorter settlement periods than gold, O'Connell noted.
Investors in the gold context broadly meant private buyers in developing countries who hedge against inflation or political and currency concerns as in India and elsewhere in the early 1990s.
The physical market needs its financial partner. The bullion market was able to move gold around the globe quickly and safely from miner to end user.
Of the top-10 producers and top-10 consumers, only the United States, China and Indonesia rate in both leading groups.
"The trade flows in the bullion market are huge and the market...is a vital lubricant in a vast machine," she said.
But the physical market has also become "vital" to mine producers to limit downside risk on their income as well as finance long-scale mine projects, she said.
